notes: \cpara{First epigraph, attributed to the \textsc{Budo Shoshinshu}, a samurai manual. I could not find the translation it quotes.}
\cpara{Second epigraph, from a book on a Japanese sword school. It supplies the post's title phrase, ``extraordinary effort.'' I could not check the quotation against the book.}
\cpara{Endorses the second epigraph from the author's own experience, and links it to ``Trying to Try'' (1 October 2008).}

\cpara{Introduces the Japanese word. The history given agrees in outline with Japanese sources. The older form, isshokenmei, referred to the land a samurai held and would defend with his life; isshōkenmei, whose first part means ``whole life'' (Jisho), developed from it (Japanese Wikipedia's article on ``isshokenmei no tochi,'' citing the \textsc{Nihon Kokugo Daijiten}). The dictionary the post links (Jeffrey's J/E Dictionary, as it reads now) gives both spellings the same everyday senses, ``very hard'' and ``with all one's might''; the difference the post reports from ``one source'' is not in it. That source, a blog page, could not be reached.}
\cpara{Praises Japanese culture on one point, having a short phrase for an all-out effort, after a warning that the West hears about the East selectively.}

\cpara{Answers a question about why self-described rationalists do not seem to do much better in life. The answer is drawn from the author's own history and offered with ``seems'': it takes ``a tremendous amount of rationality'' to stop making serious mistakes.}

\cpara{Uses Robert Aumann as the example, as the author had in ``The Dilemma: Science or Bayes?'' and ``Changing the Definition of Science'' (May 2008). Here the theorem is stated with its condition, ``with the same priors.'' The example is discussed in full in the notes on ``Crisis of Faith,'' which give Aumann's own account of his religion as ``mainly an emotional and aesthetic'' experience.}
\cpara{Asks why Japan, with ``more studious students,'' does not lead the United States in science or rule the world, as many expected in the 1980s.}
\cpara{Gives two proverbs, a Western one that rewards speaking up and a Japanese one that punishes standing out, as a short sign of the cultural difference.}

\cpara{Draws the conclusion of the comparison, and says it is not original. The inference is hedged (``this would seem to count''). Its support is one comparison between two countries, and a single pair cannot separate these traits from the many other ways Japan and the United States differ.}

\cpara{The post's main distinction, by example. A desperate effort lifts more than usual, but lifting a truck calls for something ``out of the ordinary'': methods not taught in school, difficulties outside one's routine, bypassing ``the System.''}
\cpara{A claim about the Japanese word and about Japan, resting on the comparison above.}
\cpara{Names the two virtues.}
\cpara{Ranks the second virtue above the first.}

\cpara{Weighs the cost of the higher virtue: a failed creative idea can harm bystanders, and an embezzler's ``extraordinary lengths'' are extraordinary too. The post states the risk of its own advice.}
\cpara{A story from the author's youth, with the maxim it produced: break rules only when you have ``an overwhelmingly good reason.'' It gives the reader a test for when to leave the ordinary.}

\cpara{Returns to the virtue with the author's own work. People told the author that Friendly AI (AI that would benefit humanity; the term is the author's) was futile because corporations or the military would build the first AIs. The author's reply: if one believed that, one should try for something other than the default outcome. The post grants that the two sides have ``different basic assumptions'' and does not argue them here.}

\cpara{A second case from the author's life: advice to earn degrees before expecting to be heard, answered by its cost, ``at least a ten-year detour.'' The advisers' reason, that scientists and investors would not listen otherwise, is answered in the next paragraph: the plan needs only a few private funders.}

\cpara{States the author's plan, a small, privately funded project, and the premise behind it: ``the life or death of the human species'' depends on a few people doing things that are ``at least a little extraordinary.'' The premise is stated here, not argued.}

\cpara{Sets the debate aside and reports a pattern the author often meets: a single extraordinary element ``unquestioningly taken as an absolute and unpassable obstacle.'' The cases given are the two just told, both from the author's own work.}

\cpara{Grants the case for ordinariness and asks for a sense of both the risk of the extraordinary and the cost of the ordinary. With the rule-breaking maxim above, this is the post's practical guidance.}

\cpara{Applies the point to the future: people accept a sad future because it seems ordinary, and do not ask whether it could be better. The link goes to ``Tsuyoku Naritai! (I Want To Become Stronger).''}

\cpara{Ends with an unattributed line. The ``smiling man'' is probably the Joker of \textsc{The Dark Knight}, released in July 2008. In a fan transcription of the film, he tells Harvey Dent that ``Nobody panics when things go `according to plan.' Even if the plan is horrifying!'', since horrors are accepted when ``it's all `part of the plan.' '' If that is the source, the line restates the previous paragraph: bad outcomes pass without protest when they are the expected ones.}
